questions.topic: A reserve-to-production ratio on next year's output

It means the quarry can triple its output next year before running out of material
options.misconception: reads the ratio as spare capacity

questions.explanation: The ratio divides reserves by annual output, so 30 million over 10 million gives three years of supply. Reading it as spare capacity or recovery so far mistakes duration for a volume ratio.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Discounted payback against a simple payback
questions.learningObjective: Explain why discounted payback exceeds simple payback
questions.stem: A review compares two payback methods for a retrofit project and finds that the discounted figure is longer than the simple figure. Explain why the two methods diverge and what that means for the decision.

answer.exemplar: The simple payback method treats every pound received as equally valuable whatever year it arrives in, while the discounted method values future receipts less because money received later carries opportunity cost and purchasing power risk. Because the same later cash flows are counted for less, cumulative discounted cash flow crosses zero later than cumulative undiscounted cash flow. A project that clears the simple test but not the discounted one is therefore not as secure as the simple result suggests.

questions.explanation: The simple method ignores the time value of money, while the discounted method shrinks cash flows arriving later. A later crossing means a project passing only the simple test is weaker than it looks.
questions.hint: Ask how the two methods treat cash flows arriving late.

questions.topic: Embodied energy as a share of lifetime energy
questions.learningObjective: Design a study partitioning embodied and operational energy
questions.stem: Design a study that would establish how much of the lifetime energy of a heat pump installation is embodied in manufacture rather than consumed in operation.

answer.exemplar: Gather the bill-to-gate energy for each component from supplier data, including extraction, manufacture, transport and end-of-life recycling, and add these together to obtain the embodied total. Then record metered operational electricity and heat over at least one full heating season and multiply by the modelled seasonal performance factor to get delivered heat. Expressing both totals against the same lifetime output in kilowatt hours reveals the share each occupies and any sensitivity to assumed lifetime.

questions.explanation: The study must add every stage from raw material to end of life on the supply side and measure delivered heat on the use side. Comparing raw component energy alone would miss transport effects.
questions.hint: Count bill-to-gate stages and delivered output together.

questions.topic: Water consumed by an extraction method
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two extraction methods differ in water consumption
questions.stem: An open pit operation withdraws 12 million cubic metres of water a year while an underground mine working the same orebody withdraws 3 million. Explain what drives the difference in water consumption between the two methods.

answer.exemplar: An open pit has to keep the exposed benches dewatered, because water collecting in the excavation would flood the workings and destabilise the slopes, and that dewatering demand is continuous for the life of the mine. An underground operation works below the water table and treats inflow locally, intercepting only what enters the drives. The same orebody therefore produces very different consumption totals depending on how the excavation is dewatered.

questions.explanation: Open pit dewatering must keep the whole excavated volume dry, so withdrawal is continuous and large. Underground workings intercept inflow locally.
questions.hint: Think about what each method must keep dry.

questions.topic: Discounted payback against a simple payback
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of two payback methods
questions.stem: Design a comparison that would show how sensitive a project ranking is to the choice between simple and discounted payback, using a set of candidate schemes.

answer.exemplar: Build the discounted cash flow for every candidate over its full life at the stated discount rate, then accumulate undiscounted and discounted cash flows separately year by year to find both payback points. Rank the schemes under each method and record every case where the order changes, then re-run the discounted calculation at a range of discount rates and lifetimes to see whether the reversals persist or are artefacts of one assumption. The sensitivity of the ranking, not any single payback number, is the finding.

questions.explanation: The comparison needs both cash flow series for every scheme so rankings can be compared, then a sensitivity sweep over rate and lifetime. A single project or one rate would not reveal disagreement.
questions.hint: Rank every scheme under both methods, then vary assumptions.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The share of a footprint outside a territorial boundary
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a territorial boundary frames only part of a footprint
questions.stem: A government defends its national carbon record by noting that territorial emissions fell for a sixth year. Explain why this framing understates the country's consumption-driven footprint.

answer.exemplar: Territorial emissions count only the carbon released inside the border, so they exclude the emissions released abroad to manufacture the goods and services the country imports. A fall in territorial emissions can therefore coexist with rising consumption-based emissions if imports grow or if imported goods carry more carbon than domestic ones. On a consumption basis the country's real pressure on climate is larger and possibly rising, which makes the territorial headline an incomplete basis for policy.

questions.explanation: Territorial accounting ignores the carbon released abroad to produce imported goods, so it can fall while consumption-based emissions rise. The headline describes production pressure, not consumption.
questions.hint: Ask where the carbon in imported goods was released.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Water consumed by an extraction method
questions.learningObjective: Design a study measuring water consumption by method
questions.stem: Design a measurement programme that would establish the water consumption of two competing extraction methods proposed for the same deposit.

answer.exemplar: Install flow meters on every withdrawal point and every discharge point of the pilot plant for both methods, run them under representative operating conditions for at least a full season, and record evaporation separately from other losses so that retention in tailings can be estimated rather than lumped in. Report consumption per tonne of product rather than in absolute volumes, and include a control period with the plant idle so that background inflow from rainfall and groundwater can be separated from process demand.

questions.explanation: Consumption can only be measured if withdrawal and return are metered separately and evaporative and retained losses are distinguished. Normalising per tonne makes the two methods comparable.
questions.hint: Meter inflows and outflows, and normalise per tonne.

questions.topic: Embodied energy as a share of lifetime energy
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of embodied energy in a retrofit
questions.stem: A housing provider wants to know whether insulating its stock reduces lifetime energy, given that the insulation itself consumes energy to manufacture. Design a study that would answer this without overstating the benefit.

answer.exemplar: Divide the housing stock into matched pairs of buildings similar in size, construction and occupancy, and retrofit only one building in each pair with the insulation specified. Meter heating and electricity in both buildings over at least one full heating season before and after the work to establish a measured saving, then obtain the bill-to-gate energy for the insulation from supplier data and add transport and end-of-life recycling. The net lifetime saving is the measured operational reduction only if it exceeds the embodied energy once amortised over the insulation's life.

questions.explanation: A matched-pair design with before and after metering isolates the saving, and adding the insulation's embodied energy prevents overstating the benefit. Only the net supports a lifetime reduction.
questions.hint: Use matched pairs and subtract the embodied energy.

questions.topic: A footprint accounting that shows a surplus
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a surplus-based claim for its hidden assumptions
questions.stem: A lobbying group claims a region's negative footprint balance means it has surplus carbon that can be sold to offset other sectors' emissions. Explain why this reading of the balance is unsafe.

answer.exemplar: The difference between a consumption footprint and territorial emissions is not a stock of negotiable carbon but an accounting gap produced by trade. It arises because the emissions were released where the goods were made rather than where they were consumed, and it can shrink if the country imports less or if its trading partners decarbonise their own production. Selling it as an offset also relies on the assumption that the other sector would otherwise have emitted, an additionality claim that has to be tested separately.

questions.explanation: The gap is an accounting consequence of trade, not a transferable carbon stock, and it can shrink without any change at home. Treating it as saleable offsets adds an untested additionality assumption.
questions.hint: Ask what the gap represents before treating it as an asset.

questions.topic: Discounted payback against a simple payback
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a higher discount rate on payback
questions.stem: A review raises the discount rate from 4 percent to 12 percent and finds that discounted payback lengthens while simple payback is unchanged. Explain why the two results move differently.

answer.exemplar: Simple payback sums raw cash inflows and is blind to when they arrive, so changing the discount rate cannot touch it. Discounted payback restates each inflow at present value, and a higher rate shrinks distant inflows more than near ones because the compounding penalty grows with time. With a long flow of benefits concentrated in later years, that shrinkage delays the point at which cumulative discounted inflow covers the outlay.

questions.explanation: Simple payback ignores timing entirely, so a change in the discount rate cannot affect it. Discounted payback shrinks later inflows more as the rate rises, delaying the crossing for late benefits.
questions.hint: Ask which method looks at when money arrives.

answer.exemplar: Simple payback stops counting once the outlay has been recovered, so it never notices how much the project returns after that point. The longer-payback scheme may deliver far larger net benefits over its life, and simple payback is blind to that because the counter stops. questions.learningObjective: Explain how trade affects the footprint share outside the border
questions.stem: A region claims its imported share of footprint is falling because it has cut imports. Explain why this reasoning may not hold.

answer.exemplar: A falling import volume does not guarantee a falling imported share, because the denominator matters as much as the numerator. If the domestic consumption footprint is also shrinking faster than imports, the imported share can rise even as import tonnage falls. The carbon intensity of traded goods also changes independently, since a supplier decarbonising its production lowers the imported emissions without any change in trade volumes at all.

questions.explanation: The share depends on both imported emissions and the total consumption footprint, so a fall in import tonnage need not reduce it. Trade intensity and the footprint's own movement move independently.

questions.topic: Average demand behind a peak profile
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of storage on a peak demand profile
questions.stem: A grid operator proposes batteries that store 60 megawatt hours to serve the evening peak, which lasts three hours at an average 40 megawatts above the daily average. Explain what the storage must deliver and what limits it.

answer.exemplar: The peak lasts three hours at an average 40 megawatts above the daily average, so the batteries must supply 40 megawatts for three hours, which is 120 megawatt hours of energy in total. A 60 megawatt hour installation therefore covers only half the peak if discharged fully, and it must also be recharged at some point, which either adds load overnight or requires the peak to be met partly by generation. Sizing therefore depends on the shape of the profile above the average, not on the peak alone.

questions.explanation: The energy the batteries must deliver is the excess above average multiplied by the hours the peak lasts, which here is 120 megawatt hours. A 60 megawatt hour store covers only part of it.
questions.hint: Multiply the excess by the number of peak hours.

questions.stem: A region reports a growing gap between its consumption footprint and its territorial emissions for a fifth year, driven by rising imports of manufactured goods. Explain what the trend implies about the region's carbon position.

answer.exemplar: A widening gap in the direction of imports means the region is consuming more carbon-intensive goods from elsewhere while its own domestic production becomes cleaner or contracts, so a falling territorial figure no longer signals decarbonisation of the economy. Any strategy that relies on the territorial trend to claim progress is therefore measuring the wrong thing, and the region is increasingly exposed to carbon pricing or supply shocks abroad.

questions.topic: The share of a footprint outside a territorial boundary
questions.learningObjective: Explain why consumption accounting changes policy targets
questions.stem: A government proposes to set an emission target based only on territorial emissions. Explain how a consumption accounting basis would change the policies the government must pursue.

answer.exemplar: On a consumption basis the target must be met for the carbon released in producing everything the country consumes, including imports, so policies aimed only at domestic plants leave a large and growing share of the footprint untouched. The government would need to act on procurement, on product standards and on the energy and materials used in imported goods, not merely on the power stations and factories inside its borders. Without that shift, a falling territorial number could be bought at the price of rising consumption-based emissions elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A consumption target obliges action on imports and procurement, not only on domestic plants. Territory-only policy leaves a growing part of the footprint untouched even as the headline improves.
questions.hint: Ask which emissions a territorial target actually covers.

questions.stem: A committee prefers a scheme with a two year simple payback over one with a four year discounted payback, even though the second has higher expected returns. Explain what the committee is failing to consider.

answer.exemplar: Both measures look only at the timing of cash flows under an assumption that they arrive as forecast, so neither captures the chance that they do not. A short payback gives less time for a project to disappoint before the money is returned, which makes it feel safer, yet the committee is not weighing the size of the prize, the residual value of a long-lived asset, or the risk that early flows are smaller than assumed. Choosing on payback alone systematically favours short, shallow returns over slower, larger ones.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Water consumed by an extraction method
questions.learningObjective: Explain why recycling water reduces both use and discharge
questions.stem: A plant recirculates 70 percent of its process water instead of discharging it. Explain the effect on both its water consumption and its discharge to the river.

answer.exemplar: Recirculation means the same water passes through the plant repeatedly, so each cubic metre withdrawn does more work before leaving, and the volume that must be replaced with fresh water falls sharply. The discharge to the river falls at the same time, because the water that would have been returned as effluent is now reused instead. Both the withdrawal and the load carried to the river therefore fall, but the withdrawal reduction does not translate one for one into a smaller river discharge because the water is reused rather than simply conserved.

questions.explanation: Recirculating water cuts the fresh water needed for the same output and simultaneously reduces the volume discharged to the river. Reuse and conservation are different.
questions.hint: Separate withdrawal effects from discharge effects.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Average demand behind a peak profile
questions.learningObjective: Explain why diversity of use flattens a demand profile
questions.stem: A planner notes that a district of identical houses and a district with mixed household types have different peak-to-average ratios, and the mixed district has the lower one. Explain why.

answer.exemplar: A peak-to-average ratio measures how concentrated demand is in time, and identical households share the same routines, so they cook, heat and wash at the same hours and their demand stacks into a sharp evening peak. Households with different patterns, working different hours or with children of different ages, spread their consumption across the day, so the aggregate profile is flatter. Smoothing demand in this way lets the network run closer to its average, which is cheaper and needs less peak capacity for the same total energy served.

questions.explanation: Identical households share routines and their demand stacks into a sharp peak, while varied households spread load across the day. A flatter profile lets the network run nearer its average.
questions.hint: Ask why many similar profiles stack together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Discounted payback against a simple payback
questions.learningObjective: Design a decision framework choosing between payback measures
questions.stem: Design a decision framework that would let a committee choose sensibly between two projects that rank differently under simple and discounted payback.

answer.exemplar: Set out for each project its simple payback, its discounted payback at the committee's chosen rate, the net present value over the comparison horizon and the profile of annual net cash flow, then rank on net present value as the primary criterion with payback as a risk and liquidity screen rather than a decision rule. Run the whole comparison at several discount rates and over several lifetimes to expose which conclusions are robust, and record explicitly where the two payback methods disagree so that those cases receive a stated reason for judgement rather than a silent choice.

questions.explanation: A usable framework ranks on value while using payback to expose timing and risk, and tests the ranking against other rates and lifetimes. Unexamined disagreements let an arbitrary measure decide.
questions.hint: Rank on value, then use payback as a screen.
